newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank not seen sharing mkt's dlr obsessions.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank not seen sharing mkt's dlr obsessions.

text.p: It has become almost gospel in financial markets of late that a weak mark poses the greatest challenge to German price stability and could force the central bank to lift interest rates.

But at least some heretics are questioning that belief, saying the currency market really offers little threat to German inflation and that central bank watchers will find monetary truth only by looking at other economic factors.
"What we are seeing currently is not worrying," said Eckhard Schulte, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan. "I don't think the Bundesbank has a problem with this value."
Worries that the currency market will drive the Bundesbank to raise rates has rattled short-term money market rates and contributed to a decline in the German Bund market.
On the face of it, financial markets would appear justified in their belief that the weak mark is threatening German inflation.

A weak mark raises the prospect of so-called "imported inflation", where more marks are required to buy imported goods, such as energy, that are often denominated in dollars on world markets. The mark has weakened almost 20 percent against the dollar this year to around 1.8350 to the U.S. unit.
But economists said there are many reasons to believe that Germany faces scant threat from imported inflation.

There are other factors acting to keep import prices down and there are many reasons to believe that higher import prices will not feed through into all-import consumer price inflation, analysts said.
First, the impact of the dollar on import prices is being mitigated at least marginally by lower prices for commodities and wage costs.
Second, looking at a broad range of traded goods also paints a more stable-looking Germany currency.

"In nominal terms, the mark is roughly around its reunification level and in real terms remains only slightly higher," Alison Cottrell, chief international economist at PaineWebber said in a recent commentary.
Import prices in June, the most recent month for which data are available, climbed 3.3 percent year-on-year, higher than Germany's 1.7 percent consumer price index.
The pace of import price growth, however, was not substantially higher than the pace of import price growth early this year, before the dollar started its clear upward march.
Economists said that even as the impact of the dollar's climb is not fully feeding into import prices, import price data are not fully feeding into all-important consumer price figures.
The fragile German economy, which is only now starting to recover from several years of weak growth, leaves little room for retailers to lift prices, even if their underlying costs increase.
"Currency depreciation -- as both Germany and the UK have shown -- pushes up import prices, it does not necessarily push up inflation," Cottrell said.
While economists debate the economic impact of the strong dollar, the analysis that most matters is being done at the Bundesbank.

"One should not over duly worry about the danger on import prices coming from the currency market," said Timo Klein, economist at MMS International. "The Bundesbank probably sees it that way too, but can't say so out loud."
Although the central bank has indeed openly worried about the impact of the dollar on prices, at least one council member has said there is nothing to worry about yet.

Ernst Welteke said last Friday, "The share of consumer goods that are imported and denominated in dollars is relatively small. We know that the impact of currencies on the cost of living index is exceptionally small."

Economists said the central bank is no doubt keeping a close eye on import prices, but is also nervous about broader factors like capacity utilisation which is at high levels even though the economy is growing only slowly.
